title: Heap slow-drift allocator leak triage notes
body:
Summary:

This doc captures the on-call triage for a slow heap growth issue observed across a subset of serving hosts between 2025-01-11 and 2025-01-16. Symptoms were gradual resident memory increase (~200–400MB/day on affected hosts) culminating in OOM kills on a few low-memory canary boxes. The pattern is distinct from the sudden prefetch OOMs we've seen previously: growth is incremental, correlated with a specific microbatching change (microbatch-agg v2 rollout), and reproducible with a synthetic load profile that stresses small-object allocations.

Why this is different than earlier incidents:
- Not a single thundering prefetch or KV spill; no obvious single request blob responsible.
- Growth persists across GC cycles and free lists; heap profiles show rising fragmentation and an increasing count of short-lived slab allocations that are not reclaimed as expected.
- Appears tied to async path in the new microbatch aggregation layer introduced in PR #1289 (microbatch-agg v2).

High-level timeline (local times):
- 2025-01-11 03:12 UTC: Canary host c-srv-27 reports 40% increase in RSS over 18 hours. Alert channel (sre-ops) receives memory-gauge-warning.
- 2025-01-11 08:00 UTC: SRE oncall performs initial restart of serving process — RSS drops to baseline; host returns to normal.
- 2025-01-12 22:30 UTC: Similar pattern on two more canaries; both are hosts with microbatch-agg v2 enabled.
- 2025-01-13 02:50 UTC: Local repro attempt with synthetic workload reproduces slow RSS rise (~150MB over 6 hours).
- 2025-01-14 10:14 UTC: Heap samples taken (pprof, jemalloc stats, tcmalloc-lite). Observed leaking slab classes and growth in allocation_count for 64–512B buckets.
- 2025-01-15 16:00 UTC: Hotfix toggled — rollback microbatch-agg v2 on a subset of canaries; affected hosts stabilized.
- 2025-01-16 09:20 UTC: Post-rollback monitoring shows no further slow-drifts on rolled-back hosts. Investigation proceeds.

Signals collected and what they showed:
- pprof heap profiles (safely pulled at 3 snapshots): an increasing tail of short-lived allocations pinned in thread-local caches; some thread stacks show repeated calls into async aggregator code path (agg_worker.cpp:process_batch_async).
- jemalloc stats: rising per-thread retained memory + fragmentation_index up ~12% on affected hosts.
- perf / eBPF heapwalk: allocations originate from an allocator wrapper used by microbatch aggregator when converting in-flight Request objects into compact framed buffers.
- application logs: repeated logs of `agg:queue-wait start/finish` with tight loops and occasional backpressure signals, but no long-running request.
- KV cache metrics: small uptick in cache warms but not proportional to memory growth (so unlikely to be KV cache spill).

Initial hypotheses (ranked):
1) Thread-local free list leak: the new aggregator creates many short-lived small objects on aggregator threads, and a change to the free-list draining policy in v2 prevents those thread caches from releasing back to central arena under moderate contention.
2) Unexpected retention via callback list: aggregator registers callbacks with a delayed-resolve queue; if callbacks hold references to request buffers, buffers remain live until the whole queue drains (which under certain load shapes is slow).
3) Fragmentation amplification from microbatch packing: microbatch-agg v2 packs many small frames into larger buffers with alignment padding causing more wastage in particular jemalloc bin sizes.
4) Interaction with continuous batching: aggregator interacts badly with the microbatch scheduler, causing some batches to be requeued repeatedly and memory accounting to miss drops.

Repro steps used in lab (keep for runbook):
1) Start a small pool (4 hosts) with microbatch-agg v2 toggled on.
2) Synthetic client: 250 qps of short requests (avg 12 tokens) plus a 10% spike of concurrent short bursters (100 concurrent, 0.5s spacing).
3) Observe RSS over 6–12 hours. Capture pprof snapshots every hour and jemalloc stats every 10 minutes.
4) Enable thread-level allocation tracing (sampled) to map allocation sites.

Immediate mitigations applied (and rationale):
- Rollback microbatch-agg v2 on canaries: immediate and low-risk way to stop the growth pattern while preserving production for most users.
- Increased per-thread cache drain frequency (short-term dynconfig) on a subset of hosts: reduced retained memory growth (~40% lower slope) but did not fully eliminate rise.
- Added temporary process-level cron to run periodic light GC/heap-scan every 6 hours on canaries (nonideal; only short-term mitigation).

Observed impact after mitigations:
- Hosts rolled back returned to baseline within 30–45 minutes.
- Hosts with increased cache-drain frequency showed slowed growth but still trending upward over days.
- No customer-facing errors observed; internal latency for small requests unchanged.

Deep dive notes (traces & findings):
- Allocation stack samples point to a wrapper function packFrameAndEnqueue() called from agg_worker::process_batch_async(). The wrapper allocates a framed buffer, does a copy, and enqueues to a per-thread completion queue via a lock-free ring. The ring's dequeue path defers shrink-to-fit operations to a background janitor thread.
- The janitor thread has an inactivity threshold of 30s; under our synthetic load it never crosses the threshold because the ring is frequently toggled — janitor never runs and retained buffers accumulate.
- The ring implementation keeps ownership of a small-array pool of buffers rather than returning them to central arena. That pool grows under steady high-throughput if janitor doesn't trim.
- Instrumentation proving point: adding an explicit janitor-kick after N enqueues causes immediate drop in retained memory in canary runs.

Root cause (current working hypothesis):
A combination of (a) microbatch-agg v2 introducing a per-thread enqueued-buffer pool that only trims under a janitor run, and (b) a scheduling/throughput pattern that prevents the janitor from ever running, leads to the pool growing without bound. The pool growth manifests as retained small-object allocations and eventually OOM on low-memory hosts. Secondary contributing factors include allocator fragmentation because the pool uses many different sized frames.

Short-term runbook (emergency playbook) — steps for oncall:
1) If alert memory-gauge-warning for host with microbatch-agg v2, first action: evict new canary from LB (tag=canary) and restart process. Document host id and time.
2) Check host dynconfig: if per-thread-cache-drain frequency is at default (10s), temporarily increase to 2s via dynconfig and monitor for 30m.
3) If drains reduce slope, consider rolling that dynconfig to same-arch clusters as interim.
4) If host is OOMing repeatedly or shows >1GB/day growth despite dynconfig, roll back microbatch-agg v2 on that host and rehydrate metrics.
5) Collect heap snapshots (pprof) before restart where possible and upload to CON-heap-slowdrift-2025 for continuity.

Longer-term fixes (prioritized):
- P1: Modify ring pool to have an aggressive bound and proactive trimming on enqueue when pool size > X (code change in microbatch-agg-agent). Add unit tests to simulate sustained small-frame churn.
- P1: Short-circuit janitor inactivity condition so it runs more frequently under observed production toggling patterns.
- P2: Rework frame packing to reuse a small set of fixed-size slabs rather than variable sized allocations to reduce fragmentation. Benchmark memory vs latency tradeoffs.
- P2: Add allocation telemetry (per-bin retention + per-thread retained across restarts) to the serving runtime; make alerting for per-thread retention slope > Y to catch early.
- P3: Consider swapping jemalloc tunables for small-host classes to be more aggressive about returning to OS under steady small-object churn. Validate with canaries.

Testing plan for patches:
- Unit tests: stress the ring with enqueue/dequeue patterns that historically prevented janitor runs; assert retained pool bounded.
- Integration: run canary pool with synthetic short-request traffic for 72h measuring RSS slope.
- Chaos: inject artificial delays in janitor to ensure trimming logic still prevents growth.

Open action items (owners):
- Jordan Li: create a repro harness in repo srv-tests to run the short-request workload and capture nightly heap stats (due 2025-01-20).
- Rosa Kim: prototype ring trimming logic and submit PR with tests (target 2025-01-23).
- Ethan Clarke: implement temporary dynconfig change and run fleet-wide experiment in non-prod region for 48h (target 2025-01-19).
- Priya Desai: add allocation telemetry dashboard and an alert for per-thread retention slope (target 2025-01-27).

Notes to engineers:
- Avoid quick fixes that reintroduce central locking or synchronous shrink-to-fit in hot paths. The goal is a low-latency bounded pool that returns memory reasonably to arenas.
- Consider whether the ring's lock-free ownership model is still necessary if it complicates memory lifecycle guarantees. If kept, add explicit lifecycle invariants and tests.

Retrospective/lessons learned:
- New batching code paths need targeted memory retention tests as part of PR gating (simulate long-running churn for small objects).
- Dynconfigs are useful for quick mitigation but should be design-reviewed to ensure they don't mask root causes.
- Always capture heap snapshots before restarts when possible; they were crucial here.

Appendix: quick commands (for oncall)
- pprof snapshot: curl -sS http://HOST:6060/debug/pprof/heap > /tmp/heap-$(date -u +%s).pb.gz
- jemalloc stats: sudo cat /proc/$(pidof srv-runtime)/status | grep -i jemalloc -A6
- trigger janitor kick (dev-only endpoint): curl -XPOST http://HOST:6060/internal/agg/janitor/kick

Document history:
- 2025-01-14: initial triage notes captured during oncall (JL)
- 2025-01-15: rollback and short-term mitigations (RK, EC)
- 2025-01-17: expanded root cause hypothesis and action items (JL)

Status: investigation in progress; P1 fixes prioritized and PRs expected in the next week.
